title: Area IV review: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
intro: These questions mix the eight ASEL Tasks of Area IV: normal, soft-field and short-field takeoffs and landings, the power-off 180 and the go-around. Many of them join two Tasks in one flight, the way the checkride does.

questions.q: You fly a complex single off a 2,600 ft runway with flat, open fields past the end and no obstacles. You see a positive rate of climb at about 50 ft. What do the handbooks say about raising the gear?
options: Raise it at once, because getting the drag out always comes first on any takeoff, with no exceptions
Leave it down until 1,000 ft AGL, which is the standard rule
A short delay may be warranted, since terrain absorbs energy in a gear-down forced landing
Raise it as the wheels leave the runway, before a positive rate shows
questions.why: The AFH says a delay in retracting the gear after takeoff from a short runway may be warranted, because an off-airport forced landing with the gear extended uses the energy absorbing qualities of the terrain; obstacles in the climb path are what may call for a timely retraction [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. Raising it at once is not wrong in every case, but it is not what fits this runway with open fields and no obstacles. There is no 1,000 ft rule, and the gear never comes up before a positive rate shows on the instruments [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

questions.q: You plan a normal takeoff from a field at 5,500 ft elevation. On the run-up with the mixture full rich, the engine runs rough and seems low on power. Both magnetos checked normal. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Carburetor ice; take off with carburetor heat on
Too rich for the thin air; lean it as the manufacturer recommends
This is normal at altitude; take off full rich to keep the engine cooler during the climb
The propeller is in high pitch; pull it back for takeoff
questions.why: As altitude goes up the air entering the carburetor gets thinner while the fuel does not, so the mixture gets richer. That can cause roughness and an appreciable loss of power, and it can happen on the run-up at high-elevation airports; the fix is to lean with the mixture control [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. One sample short-field chart, for example, says to lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup at fields above 3,000 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Taking off full rich here just keeps the power loss. Carburetor heat comes off when you need full power [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and the propeller belongs in low pitch (high rpm) for takeoff [[24:237|AFH 12-6]].

questions.q: You make a normal takeoff toward a ridge that rises 200 ft above field elevation. Using the AFH guidance, what is the lowest height above the field at which you should reduce from takeoff power to climb power?
options: 500 ft
300 ft
700 ft
200 ft
questions.why: The AFH says to keep takeoff power to at least 500 ft above the surrounding terrain or obstacles, because VY plus takeoff power gives the most altitude in the least time for handling an emergency [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. The ridge is 200 ft above the field, so 200 + 500 = 700 ft above the field. 500 ft would be measured from the field, not from the terrain around it. Until then the commercial standard is VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS CA.IV.A.S13).

questions.q: The examiner names a point 750 ft past the landing threshold for three landings: a normal landing, a short-field landing and a power-off 180. What is the farthest touchdown from the threshold that meets the commercial standard for each?
options: Normal 1,150 ft, short-field 950 ft, power-off 180 1,150 ft
Normal 950 ft, short-field 850 ft, power-off 180 950 ft
Normal 950 ft, short-field 950 ft, power-off 180 850 ft
Normal 850 ft, short-field 850 ft, power-off 180 950 ft
questions.why: The commercial ACS allows on the point or within 200 ft beyond it for a normal landing (ACS CA.IV.B.S10) and for a power-off 180 (ACS CA.IV.M.S8), but only 100 ft for a short-field landing (ACS CA.IV.F.S10). So 750 + 200 = 950 ft, 750 + 100 = 850 ft and 750 + 200 = 950 ft. The 1,150 and 950 ft answer uses the private windows for normal and short-field landings (400 and 200 ft, ACS PA.IV.B.S10 and PA.IV.F.S10); the power-off 180 is not a private Task. Landing short of the point fails all three.

questions.q: Your airplane's demonstrated crosswind is 15 knots. The airport has Runways 36 and 9. The wind is 060 at 24 knots. Which choice fits the lessons?
options: Runway 36: about 12 knots of crosswind, inside the demonstrated value
Runway 9: about 12 knots of crosswind and about 21 knots of headwind
Runway 36: about 21 knots of crosswind, but the demonstrated value is not a limit, so fly it wing-low
Runway 9: about 21 knots of crosswind, so divert
questions.why: A crosswind component chart splits the wind into crosswind and headwind parts [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Runway 36 is 60 degrees off the wind: 24 x sin 60 = 20.8, about 21 knots of crosswind, above the 15-knot value. Runway 9 is 30 degrees off: 24 x sin 30 = 12 knots of crosswind and 24 x cos 30 = 20.8, about 21 knots of headwind. You must know the airplane's crosswind component and stay within it, and when the wind is too strong for one runway, land on a better one [[24:190|AFH 9-19]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. The demonstrated value is not a published limit, but that does not make 21 knots a good plan: exceeding the demonstrated crosswind is a listed crosswind error [[24:191|AFH 9-20]], and here a more favorable runway is available. The 12-knot figure for Runway 36 swaps the two components.

questions.q: You learned to fly on a 50 ft wide runway. Today you fly a normal approach to a 150 ft wide runway at a large airport. Which pair, the likely error and a guard against it, matches the lessons?
options: You feel higher than you are and fly too low, so fly a steeper approach than usual to make up for the illusion and trust your sight picture
You feel lower than you are and land short, so carry 10 knots of extra speed
A wide runway can make you level off high and land hard; check the altimeter often and use a VASI or PAPI if there is one
Width illusions only happen at night, so no guard is needed in daylight
questions.why: A narrower-than-usual runway makes you feel higher than you are and leads to a low approach. A wider-than-usual runway has the opposite effect, with the risk of leveling off high and landing hard or overshooting the runway [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. To guard against illusions, check the airport diagram and Chart Supplement, check the altimeter often and use a VASI or PAPI when there is one [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]]. The 'too low' answer is the narrow runway case, extra speed only adds float, and the PHAK does not limit the width illusion to night.

questions.q: You land on a muddy strip to pick up a passenger and will take off again from the same strip. Which plan fits both the soft-field landing and soft-field takeoff lessons?
options: Brake to a stop at the far end, turn around and do the run-up there
Brake lightly to slow down, then do the run-up while rolling slowly
Stop on the runway centerline for the run-up so the takeoff starts from the very beginning and uses all the runway available
Keep rolling with power to firm ground, do the run-up there, then taxi onto the runway and line up without stopping
questions.why: After a soft-field landing, brakes should be avoided because they load the nose gear and can make the nose wheel dig in, and you may need more power just to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. All run-up and before-takeoff items should be done before taxiing onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], and for the takeoff you keep a continuous motion with enough power while lining up, since stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Stopping on the runway for the run-up is exactly the stop that can get you stuck.

questions.q: On a short-field takeoff the airplane wants to lift off well before VX. On a soft-field takeoff it flies itself off below a safe climb speed. What do the lessons say to do in each case?
options: Short-field: hold it on the ground with forward pressure until VX. Soft-field: level off in ground effect until reaching VX
Short-field: let it fly. Soft-field: hold it on the surface until VY
In both: climb at once at the lift-off speed to get out of ground effect
In both: let it fly, level off just clear of the surface in ground effect, and accelerate to at least VX
questions.why: For the short-field takeoff, the AFH says to let such an airplane lift off in ground effect, lower the pitch to level with the wheels just clear of the runway and accelerate to VX, which the AFH prefers to holding it on the ground with forward elevator pressure [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. For the soft-field takeoff, it flies off below a safe climb speed, you lower the nose gently and stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Climbing out of ground effect below the recommended climb speed gives much less climb performance [[24:143|AFH 6-11]], and the airplane tends to settle back onto the surface [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

questions.q: A turf strip runs 18/36. The Chart Supplement shows it slopes uphill toward the south end, so a takeoff on Runway 18 is uphill. The wind is 360 at 6 knots. Which runway gives the shorter soft-field takeoff, and why?
options: Runway 36, because the downslope helps acceleration and the wind is a headwind
Runway 18, because the upslope helps you rotate sooner and the wind is only 6 knots
Runway 18, because the tailwind gives a higher groundspeed sooner
Either one, because the slope and the wind cancel out
questions.why: An upsloping runway slows acceleration and gives a longer ground run; a downsloping runway aids acceleration and shortens the takeoff [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. A tailwind makes the airplane reach a higher groundspeed before it gets to lift-off speed, so it lengthens the takeoff; a tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed adds about 21 percent [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Runway 36 is downhill and into the wind, so both factors help. On Runway 18 both factors hurt, so nothing cancels.

questions.q: Your POH lists a normal approach speed of 70 knots and a short-field approach speed of 61 knots. The wind is calm. For a soft-field landing on your commercial checkride, what target and window do you fly on final?
options: 70 knots, from 65 to 75 knots
61 knots, from 56 to 71 knots
61 knots, from 56 to 66 knots
66 knots, to allow for float in ground effect
questions.why: The AFH says the final approach speed for short-field landings is equally right for soft-field landings, and that higher speeds can cause excessive float in ground effect [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The commercial ACS then allows ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7), so 61 - 5 = 56 to 61 + 5 = 66 knots. The 56 to 71 window is the private +10/-5 band. Adding speed for the float is backwards: extra speed is what makes the float.

questions.q: On the checkride the examiner asks for a soft-field landing on a turf runway. Which statement describes the commercial touchdown standard for this Task?
options: On or within 100 ft beyond a specified point
On or within 200 ft beyond a specified point
On or within 400 ft beyond a specified point
A suitable point for the wind, surface and obstructions, with proper pitch, minimum sink rate, no side drift and alignment with the runway center; no distance tolerance is given
questions.why: The soft-field Task asks you to pick and aim for a touchdown point that suits the wind, landing surface and obstructions (ACS CA.IV.D.S5), and to touch down at a proper pitch attitude with minimum sink rate, no side drift and the longitudinal axis aligned with the center of the runway (ACS CA.IV.D.S10). Unlike the normal (200 ft) and short-field (100 ft) landings, it gives no distance tolerance. The goal is to touch down as smoothly as possible at the slowest possible speed [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

questions.q: You fly a soft-field takeoff from a sandy strip and later the same day a soft-field landing back on it. Which idea runs through both, according to the lessons?
options: Use back pressure and power so the wings, not the wheels, carry the weight: early on takeoff, as long as practical on landing
Keep the nose wheel firmly on the surface for steering until the speed is low
Use light, steady braking so the speed stays under control
Climb out steeply right after lift-off and fly a steep final, to spend as little time as possible near the soft surface and the mud
questions.why: On the soft-field takeoff the goal is to move the weight from the wheels to the wings as early as possible [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. On the soft-field landing the wings support the weight as long as practical, and back-elevator pressure and power control how fast it moves to the wheels [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Holding the nose wheel down or braking loads the nose gear and can make it dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Steep is wrong both ways: after a soft-field lift-off you stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and there is no reason for a steep descent unless obstacles are present [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

questions.q: You plan a short-field takeoff at a field with a pressure altitude of 4,000 ft and an outside air temperature of 27 °C. Using the IFH estimate, about what is the density altitude, and what does it do to the takeoff?
options: About 6,400 ft; you lift off at a lower indicated airspeed in the thin air, which saves a good deal of runway
About 7,240 ft; you lift off at a higher indicated airspeed
About 4,400 ft; the takeoff is close to the chart's standard-day number
About 6,400 ft; same indicated lift-off speed but higher true airspeed, so the roll is longer
questions.why: Standard temperature falls about 2 °C per 1,000 ft from 15 °C [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]], so standard at 4,000 ft is 15 - 8 = 7 °C. The IFH adds about 120 ft for every degree above standard [[23:83|IFH 4-6]]: 27 - 7 = 20 degrees, 20 x 120 = 2,400 ft, and 4,000 + 2,400 = 6,400 ft. At altitude the airplane lifts off at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level, but the true airspeed is greater [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]], and thin air also cuts power, thrust and lift [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]]. 7,240 ft comes from multiplying the whole 27 degrees instead of the difference from standard.

questions.q: You will make a short-field landing at a 2,400 ft strip and a short-field takeoff from it later. Which statement about safety margins is supported by the lessons?
options: Add at least 15 percent to computed landing distance; no takeoff margin is given, so set your own with your CFI
AC 91-79B requires 15 percent on both takeoff and landing distances
No margin is needed if you fly exactly the chart technique
Add 15 percent to the takeoff distance only, because the POH landing number already includes a margin for average pilot skill
questions.why: AC 91-79B says to add a safety margin of at least 15 percent once the landing distance is determined [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. That AC is about landing, and none of the lesson sources gives a takeoff margin, so the lessons tell you to set a personal one. Flying the chart technique is no guarantee: chart numbers come from a new airplane flown with average skill [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. The last choice gets it backwards: the AC margin is for landing distance, not takeoff [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]].

questions.q: On a short-field takeoff roll the rpm is right, the engine gauges are normal and you are on centerline, but 300 ft into the roll the airspeed indicator still reads zero. What does the REACT check call for?
options: Continue, rotate at the usual attitude, and check GPS groundspeed and the other engine gauges after lift-off, since they are normal
Abort: idle power, maximum braking with directional control, announce on tower or CTAF, exit the runway, then find out why
Keep rolling to your takeoff point, then decide
Abort, then stop on the runway to troubleshoot the pitot system
questions.why: In the REACT check, A means airspeed continually increasing. If any REACT item is not as expected, abort, announce on tower or CTAF that you are aborting, exit the runway, taxi to a safe area and figure out why [[16:11|AC 90-48E 10.4.2]]. To reject, reduce power to idle and apply maximum braking while keeping directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. The takeoff point (T) is the last place to be airborne, not a place to wait for before acting on a bad item, and stopping on the runway leaves you in the way of traffic.

questions.q: Your POH gives 70 knots for a normal approach and 63 knots for a short-field approach. The wind is 18 gusting 26. Taking the gust factor as gust minus steady wind and adding half of it, which airspeed on short final is inside the commercial window for the short-field landing but too slow for the normal landing?
options: 68 knots
61 knots
71 knots
75 knots
questions.why: Neither the AFH nor the ACS defines the gust factor, so taking it as gust minus steady wind is an application, as the question says: 26 - 18 = 8 knots, and half is 4. Pilots often add half the gust factor on a normal approach [[24:191|AFH 9-20]], and no more than half on a short-field approach [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]; adding half to both, so the targets are 70 + 4 = 74 knots (normal) and 63 + 4 = 67 knots (short-field). With ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.B.S7, CA.IV.F.S7) the windows are 69 to 79 and 62 to 72. Only 68 knots is inside 62 to 72 but below 69. 71 knots fits both windows, 75 fits only the normal one and 61 is too slow for both.

questions.q: Tomorrow you land at a 5,000 ft field on a dry 2,200 ft runway (code 6). Your POH short-field chart, worked for that elevation, temperature and weight, gives 1,380 ft total over a 50 ft obstacle, dry and unfactored. You have no other landing data, so you use AC 91-79B Table 3-1 for the time-of-arrival check. What landing distance is required, and does it fit?
options: Yes: 1,380 x 1.15 is about 1,587 ft, well inside 2,200 ft
No: 1,380 x 1.67 x 1.15 is about 2,650 ft
No: 1,380 x 1.67 is about 2,305 ft, more than the 2,200 ft runway
Yes: the chart is already for 5,000 ft, so on a dry runway 1,380 ft needs no factor
questions.why: The chart number is already longer than a sea level one, because you land at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. With no manufacturer or data provider advisory data, the AC says to multiply the dry, unfactored AFM/POH distance by the Table 3-1 factor for the conditions on arrival [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. The reciprocating factor for a dry runway (code 6) is 1.67 [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]: 1,380 x 1.67 = 2,304.6, about 2,305 ft, more than 2,200 ft. The factors already include the 15 percent margin [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]], so multiplying by 1.15 again double counts it, and 1.15 alone or no factor leaves out what the table method requires.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the short-field and soft-field landings?
options: The soft-field final is flown faster than the short-field final to allow for float
Same final approach speed, but the short-field ends in maximum braking while the soft-field avoids the brakes
The short-field landing is held 1 to 2 ft off the surface with power while the speed bleeds off, then lowered to the runway
Both end with maximum braking once the nose wheel is down
questions.why: The short-field final approach speed is equally right for a soft-field landing [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. In the short-field landing you touch down at minimum controllable airspeed with little float and then apply maximum braking once the nose wheel is down [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. In the soft-field landing you hold the airplane 1 to 2 ft up with some power while the speed bleeds off [[24:194|AFH 9-23]], and avoid the brakes, which can make the nose wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Flying the soft-field final faster only adds float.

questions.q: At 200 ft on a power-off 180 you can see you will touch down about 300 ft past the examiner's point. Which response goes against both the AFH guidance and the ACS?
options: Lower the nose and force the wheels onto the runway near the point
Go around and tell the examiner
Make a good, normal landing past the point
Go around, then fly another approach to the point if the examiner asks for one
questions.why: Forcing the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting the spot is on the AFH list of common errors, and the AFH says it is always better to make a good landing away from the spot than a poor one on it [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. The ACS note for this Task says neither you nor the examiner may force a landing to finish it (ACS Appendix 3). A go-around or a long landing will not meet the 200 ft tolerance (ACS CA.IV.M.S8), but both are safe choices. Forcing it on is the one that breaks the rules.

questions.q: On a normal approach (CA.IV.B) and on a power-off 180 (CA.IV.M), you find yourself low. Which pair of fixes matches the lessons?
options: Normal: raise the nose to stretch the glide. Power-off: add a little power
Both: retract the flaps partway to cut drag
Normal: retract some flaps. Power-off: raise the nose to stretch the glide

Normal: add power and raise the nose together to meet the path, then reduce power and pitch down. Power-off: dog-leg toward the runway on base and delay flaps; never stretch the glide or retract flaps
questions.why: On a normal approach, a low airplane meets the glide path by raising the pitch and adding power to level off while holding speed, then reducing power and pitching down to stay on the path; retracting flaps for an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. In a power-off approach the throttle stays closed, so you shape the path instead: dog-leg toward the runway on base and use late flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Never try to stretch the glide or retract the flaps to reach the spot, and using the throttle to extend the glide is a listed error [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

questions.q: You train for the power-off 180 in a single-engine turboprop. At flight idle it sinks far too fast, and the manufacturer's checklist calls for feathering the propeller after a real engine failure. What does the AFH say to do in training?
options: Feather the propeller so the glide is realistic
Fly it at flight idle and fix the steep glide by flying a closer base leg and a shorter final
Set enough power to match the performance of a feathered propeller
Shut the engine down at altitude to practice the real glide
questions.why: The AFH notes that some single-engine turboprops descend too fast at flight idle. In training and on a checkride, the propeller is not feathered; instead the pilot sets enough power to give the performance expected with the propeller feathered [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Flying at flight idle trains a glide the airplane would not have after a real failure, and feathering or shutting down in training is exactly what the AFH avoids.

questions.q: On a normal landing you get a severe bounce and the airspeed is low. What go-around do the lessons describe?
options: Hold the nose high and add a little power to cushion the next touchdown, then land
Close the throttle and brake firmly to stop the bounce
Full power and pitch straight to the VY attitude to get away from the runway
Full power, keep straight and lower the nose to a safe climb attitude; accept a few moments of level flight to gain speed, and if it touches again, hold a constant, safe pitch and keep going
questions.why: After a severe bounce the safest action is an immediate go-around: full power, directional control and the nose lowered to a safe climb attitude. Do not try to land from a bad bounce, because speed bleeds off fast in the nose-high attitude and a stall may come before the next touchdown [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]. From a low-speed start, the first priority is control and flying speed, and a few moments of level or near level flight may be needed to accelerate [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. If it settles and bounces early in the go-around, keep it straight with a constant, safe pitch; the power cushions the next contact [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Pitching straight to VY with no airspeed risks a stall [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: You go around in a turbocharged single with a constant-speed propeller. How do you set go-around power?
options: Propeller control full forward (rpm first), then the throttle smoothly to the maximum allowable manifold pressure while watching the engine gauges
Throttle in quickly first, then bring the propeller control forward
Push the throttle abruptly to the stop, because the turbocharger needs a fast input
Leave the propeller control where it is; the governor raises rpm by itself
questions.why: Maximum takeoff power means the propeller control all the way forward (low pitch, high rpm) and the throttle to the maximum allowable manifold pressure [[24:236|AFH 12-5]]. When increasing power, increase rpm first and then manifold pressure [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. On turbocharged engines all power control movements should be slow and smooth, because abrupt throttle movements raise the chance of overboosting, and you should watch the engine gauges [[24:241|AFH 12-10]]. That still fits the go-around rule of full power smoothly and without hesitation [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: VFR at a towered airport, the tower says: 'N123AB, go around.' No other instructions follow. What do you do?
options: Turn right away onto the downwind leg to save time
Overfly the runway climbing to pattern altitude, then enter on the crosswind leg
Climb straight ahead to 1,000 ft above pattern altitude and hold there until the tower calls you
Turn early across the pattern to keep the runway in sight
questions.why: 'Go around' tells you to abandon the approach, and more instructions may follow. Unless ATC says otherwise, a VFR aircraft overflies the runway while climbing to pattern altitude and enters the pattern via the crosswind leg [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]. You may not operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised, except in an emergency [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]. An early turn to downwind or across the pattern cuts into traffic that is expecting you on the upwind and crosswind legs.
